plan.title: If Nobody Uses Cash... Why Is There More Of It Than Ever?
alt_titles: Where Did All The $100 Bills Go?
plan.description:
Cash is used for only 14% of US payments, yet there is more paper money than ever: $2.3 trillion, most of it in $100 bills. Here is where it goes, why people hold it, and who benefits.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:54 The cash paradox
1:56 The hundred dollar takeover
3:58 Where the hundreds go
5:23 Cash follows fear
6:33 Who wins
7:36 What it means for you

segments.narration: Nobody uses cash anymore. You probably tap a card or your phone for almost everything.
So here's a question that should not have an answer. If nobody uses cash, why is there more of it than ever?
At the end of 2024, there was two point three trillion dollars of American paper money out in the world.
That's fifty-five billion individual notes. Seven for every person on the planet.
And the number isn't shrinking. It goes up almost every single year.
Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve says cash was used for just fourteen percent of payments in 2024.
Credit cards took thirty-five percent. Debit cards took thirty.
So someone is holding trillions of dollars in cash that they are not spending at the shops.
And when I went looking for who that someone is, the answer turned out to be a lot stranger than people stuffing money under the mattress.
It involves the most popular banknote in the world, a printing budget worth billions, and a lot of money that has quietly left the country.
To understand it, we need to start with the boring part. How much cash people actually use.
Every year, the Federal Reserve asks thousands of Americans to keep a diary of every single payment they make.
In 2024, the average person still made about seven cash payments a month.
That number has not changed since 2020. Cash isn't dying. It's just stuck.
It's still the third most used way to pay, behind credit and debit cards, and it has been for five years.
And here's the odd part. Nearly two thirds of those cash payments were made by people who say they'd rather pay some other way.
They don't love cash. They just use it when the card machine is down, when the place is cash only, or when they're splitting a bill.
Nearly eighty percent of people held some cash for at least one day of the month, in every one of these surveys since 2018.
And more than ninety percent say they expect to keep using cash, either to pay or to store value.
That last bit, to store value, is the clue. Because people aren't keeping fives and tens. They're keeping something else.
Let's look at what's actually out there. Not in dollars, but in notes.
In 2015, there were about thirty-eight billion American banknotes in circulation.
Ten years later, at the end of 2025, there were fifty-six point six billion.
That's an increase of almost half, in the same decade that phones replaced wallets.
Now, the one dollar bill did grow, from eleven point four billion notes to fifteen point two billion.
But the hundred dollar bill nearly doubled. From ten point eight billion notes to nineteen point nine billion.
Which means there are now more hundred dollar bills in existence than one dollar bills.
Think about how often you've actually held a hundred dollar bill. Now think about how often you've held a one.
Something about that doesn't add up, and that's because most hundreds are not being used to buy things.
By value, the gap is even more extreme. The hundreds alone are worth nearly two trillion dollars.
At the end of 2024, they made up one point nine trillion of the two point three trillion dollars out there.
In other words, more than eighty percent of all American cash, by value, is hundreds.
A researcher at the Saint Louis Fed looked at this trend and put it bluntly. The recent growth in cash is due solely to the rise in hundred dollar bills.
And the Fed keeps printing them. For 2025, it ordered between seven hundred fifty-two million and eight hundred sixty-seven million new hundred dollar notes.
Each one costs about eleven cents to print, and has a face value of a hundred dollars.
And it's not a rounding error in the budget. The whole 2025 order was worth somewhere between eighty-three and a hundred and thirteen billion dollars at face value.
Up to eighty-seven billion of that was hundreds. The twenties, the bill that actually comes out of ATMs, could be as low as zero.
On top of the per note cost, the Fed budgeted six hundred eighty-eight million dollars of fixed printing costs for the year.
That's a serious amount of money to spend on a product that, supposedly, nobody uses.
So who wants a stack of paper that pays zero interest, can be stolen, and loses value to inflation every year?
A lot of people. Most of them just don't live here.
Measuring where cash goes is hard. Nobody tracks a banknote after it leaves the bank.
When a bank needs more cash, it orders it from the Federal Reserve. When it has too much, it sends it back.
If the money goes out and never comes back, it's somewhere. Either in someone's home, or in someone's suitcase.
But the Federal Reserve has spent decades trying, using shipping records, seasonal patterns, and even the wear and tear on returned notes.
The US government's own currency site says that as much as half the value of American cash is estimated to be circulating abroad.
An economist at the Federal Reserve, Ruth Judson, estimated that before 1990, around twenty percent of US cash was held abroad.
By her later work, that had climbed to between fifty and sixty percent.
And for hundred dollar bills specifically, as much as seventy percent were held outside the United States in 2011.
Why would someone in another country want American paper money?
Because in a lot of places, the local currency is the risk. If prices double, your savings in the local money can be cut in half.
A US hundred dollar bill is the opposite. It's small, it's recognised almost everywhere, and it has held its value better than most.
It's not a payment method there. It's a savings account you can hold in your hand.
And because it's paper, it doesn't need a bank account, a phone signal or a working payment network. It just needs to be trusted.
And that's the same reason people hoard cash at home, just on a much bigger scale.
Look at when cash demand jumps. It doesn't follow shopping. It follows fear.
At the end of 2007, right before the financial crisis, there was seven hundred sixty-two billion dollars of US cash, about five percent of the economy.
By the end of 2018, it had more than doubled to one point six trillion, close to eight percent of the economy.
So during the decade that card payments took over, cash grew faster than the economy itself.
And it kept going. The hundreds were worth one point seven seven trillion dollars in 2021, and nearly two trillion by 2025.
When banks look shaky or the world feels uncertain, people don't want an app balance. They want something physical.
That's also why cash still matters most to people with the least room for error.
The Fed's diary found that households earning under twenty-five thousand dollars a year, and adults over fifty-five, rely on cash more than anyone else.
For them it's a budget tool. You can see exactly how much is left, and there's no overdraft fee.
And when the power goes out or the card network fails, cash is the only thing that still works at the checkout.
That's why so many people who say they prefer cards still keep a few notes in their wallet. It's a backup system.
So who actually benefits from all this paper?
Think about what a banknote is. It's a promise from the Federal Reserve that it pays no interest on.
When someone abroad holds a hundred dollar bill for twenty years, the United States has essentially been handed real goods and services in exchange for an eleven cent piece of paper.

A Saint Louis Fed analysis estimated that if all the growth in hundred dollar bills came from foreign demand, it would explain about a quarter of the rise in the Fed's liabilities since the financial crisis.
That's a quiet, interest free loan from the rest of the world. And it keeps growing every year.
Compare that with a bank. If you leave money in a savings account, the bank pays you something for it. Cash pays you nothing.
So every year a hundred dollar bill sits in a drawer, its owner gives up the interest they could have earned. That's the real price of feeling safe.
And inflation takes a cut too. A hundred dollar bill buys less every year, but it's still a hundred dollar bill, so it never feels like a loss.
So here's the answer to the paradox.
What does this mean for you? Probably that the cashless future people keep predicting is further away than it looks.
Card payments will keep winning at the checkout. But as long as people around the world don't trust their banks or their currency, demand for paper dollars will keep growing.
It also means the cash in circulation tells you more about fear than about shopping. When that number jumps, people are nervous.
And if you are one of the people keeping a stack at home, you're in good company. You're just paying for that comfort in lost interest.
Nobody uses cash, at least not at the checkout. But a huge number of people still hold it, as insurance, as savings, and as an escape hatch from a currency they don't trust.
The cash in your wallet is the small part of the story. The real story is a two trillion dollar pile of hundreds, much of it sitting in drawers and safes far from America.
Cash didn't die. It just stopped being money you spend, and became money you keep.
If you want more stories about where money really goes, subscribe. Thanks for watching.
